nameStory: Field penny-cress gets its charming name from its distinctive flat, round seed pods that look remarkably like old-fashioned pennies dangling from the stem. The 'field' part of the name hints at where you'll most likely encounter this little wanderer - in disturbed soils, farm fields, and other open areas where it thrives as a opportunistic weed.
description: Field penny-cress is a small annual herb in the mustard family that typically grows 6 inches to 2 feet tall. It produces clusters of tiny white four-petaled flowers at the top of its stems, followed by its most distinctive feature - flat, round seed pods that really do look like little coins. The plant has a somewhat weedy appearance with simple leaves and an upright, branching growth habit that makes it easy to overlook until you notice those peculiar penny-like pods.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, round seed pods about the size of a penny with a distinctive notch at the top - they're papery thin and make a subtle rattling sound when shaken in the breeze

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with four petals arranged in small clusters at stem tips - each flower is only about 1/8 inch across but they're numerous

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are oval with shallow teeth along the edges, while upper leaves clasp the stem with small ear-like projections - they have a slightly waxy feel

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual herb that branches near the top, often forming small colonies in disturbed areas - the whole plant has a somewhat sparse, weedy appearance

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: When crushed, leaves and stems give off a sharp, slightly garlicky mustard family smell that's quite distinctive

habitat: Field penny-cress thrives in disturbed soils throughout New England, particularly in agricultural fields, roadsides, waste areas, and construction sites. It prefers full sun and well-drained soils, often appearing in areas where the ground has been recently tilled or otherwise disturbed. You'll rarely find it in undisturbed natural areas, as it depends on human activity to create the open, sunny conditions it needs.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge early and begin flowering in late spring with small clusters of white blooms. Young plants are easiest to identify by their distinctive leaf arrangement.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs in early summer, followed by the development of the characteristic penny-shaped seed pods. The distinctive flat pods are fully formed and most noticeable during this season.
seasonality.fall: Mature seed pods turn brown and papery, eventually splitting open to release seeds. Plants begin to die back as annual life cycle completes.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist with dried seed pods still attached, but living plants are absent as this is an annual species.

funFact: Field penny-cress seeds can remain viable in soil for over 20 years, which explains why this European native can suddenly appear in gardens and fields where it's never been seen before - the 'pennies' from decades past finally decided to cash in!
confusionNotes: The small white flowers might be confused with other mustard family members, but no other plant in New England produces those distinctive flat, round, penny-shaped seed pods. Memory trick: if it looks like someone scattered coins on the plant, you've found penny-cress!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being considered a weed in most situations, field penny-cress is actually edible and has been used as a potherb in some cultures, though it has a strong, peppery flavor typical of the mustard family. However, it's best admired rather than eaten unless you're certain of your identification.
compareHints: Field penny-cress is the only Thlaspi species commonly found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Among other mustard family members, it's distinguished by those unmistakable flat, circular seed pods - shepherd's purse has heart-shaped pods, while garlic mustard has long, narrow pods that look nothing like pennies.
